clue.text: Good for a stretch in one castle perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps says the letters of the castle and the one may be arranged some other way

parts.note: one is the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A knight finds a castle a good place for a long stay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' is the anagram signal: I (one) with CASTLE is rearranged. 'in' just joins the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic material is valued because it will stretch and spring back.

clue.text: Results coming in when Sue says so

indicators.note: coming in says the word arrives inside the run of letters that follows

explanation.surface: Election results are announced whenever Sue gives the word.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'whEN SUE Says'; 'so' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Ensues means follows on as a consequence, the way outcomes do.

clue.text: A traveller by air

parts.note: a person who flies; viator is also Latin for a traveller, after an A

explanation.definitionFit: A pilot is someone who journeys through the sky in a plane.

clue.text: The Spanish cry in ecstasy for freedom from bigotry

indicators.note: in says the Spanish cry sits inside the word for ecstasy

parts.note: a trance is a rapt, ecstatic state
ole is the Spanish shout of approval at a bullfight

explanation.surface: A Spaniard's shout of joy celebrates freedom from prejudice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Spanish' tempts you toward EL, but the cry is the bullring's shout; 'in' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerance is the willingness to accept other views, the opposite of prejudice.

clue.text: DORA Section involved latitude and longitude

indicators.note: involved means tangled up, so the letters are mixed

parts.note: taken as written: the Defence of the Realm Act

explanation.surface: A wartime act's section covers lines on the map.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involved' is the anagram signal on DORA plus SECTION. DORA was the Defence of the Realm Act, Britain's First World War emergency law.
explanation.definitionFit: A position on Earth is given by a pair of grid numbers, the two angles of a map reference.

clue.text: Went by sea-possibly East Mediterranean

indicators.note: possibly says the letters given by East and Med may be rearranged

parts.note: the Med is the usual short name for the Mediterranean Sea

explanation.surface: A traveller reports sailing, perhaps in the eastern Mediterranean.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' tells you to rearrange EAST plus MED, the short name for the Mediterranean.
explanation.definitionFit: Ships powered by boilers steamed across the water, so to have steamed is to have sailed.

clue.text: Uncle raises mother's boy

indicators.note: in a down answer, raises means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: ma is mother, so mother's is MA'S

explanation.surface: An uncle brings up his sister's son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raises' turns MAS upwards; Uncle Sam personifies the United States, and 'boy' links (Sam is also a boy's name).
explanation.definitionFit: Uncle Sam is the bearded figure standing for the US government.

clue.text: Besides, I included a girl

indicators.note: included says the I goes inside the word for besides

parts.note: else means besides, otherwise

explanation.surface: A list adds that, as well as others, a girl was included.
explanation.walkthrough: 'included' puts I inside ELSE (besides).
explanation.definitionFit: Elsie is a female first name.

clue.text: Russian cocktail

definitions.meaning: a petrol bomb in a bottle, named after that minister

explanation.definitionFit: A Soviet statesman whose name was given to the improvised petrol bomb.

clue.text: Causes ruin of the French story possibly

parts.note: des is French for of the, plural

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of story may be rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic says a French tale might be ruinous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of the French' is the plural French article with 'of', not LE or LA; 'possibly' signals the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: To wreck something completely is to bring ruin on it.

clue.text: Housekeeper's store not yet full it seems

definitions.meaning: a room in a big house where the housekeeper kept preserves, cordials and the like
read as two words, there is space left over, so a place is not yet full

explanation.definitionFit: In a country house the housekeeper's pantry for jams and liqueurs bore this name; split in two it says space remains.

clue.text: Sedimentary blocks ?

parts.note: deposits of fine river mud that choke channels, the word serving as both the noun for the deposit and the verb for clogging

explanation.definitionFit: Fine sediment carried by water settles out and clogs harbours and channels, which it is said to do as it builds up.

clue.text: Come in, No 12, this is your finish

indicators.note: addressed to the light numbered twelve, saying this entry is that word's ending, so its opening letters are dropped

parts.note: the answer to the clue numbered 12 across, the nonconformist

explanation.surface: An official calls a contestant in, telling them their turn is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No 12' points to 12 across, DISSENTER; 'this is your finish' says this answer is its tail, so drop DISS from the front.
explanation.definitionFit: To go into a room is to step inside it, as a summons to come in invites.

clue.text: Nonconformist breaks Sid's record

indicators.note: breaks tells you to smash the letters of Sid's and rebuild them

parts.note: the possessive is spelt with its S here, the letters SIDS
to record something in a ledger is to enter it

explanation.surface: A rebel athlete beats Sid's best time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaks' and 'record' read as athletics, but 'breaks' is the anagram signal and 'record' is the verb, as in writing into a ledger.
explanation.definitionFit: Historically a Protestant outside the Church of England was a Dissenter, a nonconformist.

clue.text: Making getaway after breaking desk — confusing

indicators.note: after says the confusing word comes behind the broken desk
breaking tells you to smash the letters of desk

parts.note: addling means muddling or confusing

explanation.surface: A thief flees after smashing a desk, causing confusion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking' is the anagram signal and 'after' puts the confusing word at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Skedaddle is informal for run away hastily, so skedaddling is fleeing.

clue.text: Artillery maps ?

parts.note: ordnance is a word for heavy guns and military supplies
to survey land is to measure and chart it

explanation.surface: A clue asking whether gunners draw maps.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ordnance Survey is Britain's national mapping agency, founded to map the country for military use.
explanation.definitionFit: Britain's official map-making body began under the Board of Ordnance, the army's supply office.

clue.text: Craftily lures Ivan 'into this joint

definitions.note: the answer comes before joint to name a coupling, so the adjective stands for the joint

indicators.note: craftily suggests artful rearranging, so the letters are shuffled

explanation.surface: A temptress slyly lures Ivan into her club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craftily' is the anagram signal; 'into this joint' asks for the word that goes before 'joint' to name the flexible coupling in a car's drive shaft.
explanation.definitionFit: A coupling that lets a shaft turn at any angle is called a universal joint.

clue.text: Relates to these businesses

explanation.definitionFit: Is about, as a story is about something; also commercial firms.

clue.text: Arrangements for speeches about the Treasury ? Right

indicators.note: about says the speeches go around the following pieces

parts.note: orations are formal speeches
a chest is where treasure or funds are kept, a treasury

explanation.surface: A clue asking about preparations for ministers' speeches on Treasury matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' is the container signal; the Treasury is a strongbox of funds, not the government department.
explanation.definitionFit: Orchestrating music means scoring it for instruments, so the results are musical arrangements.

clue.text: The colonel gets many letters ? A heap

parts.note: CO is a commanding officer, such as the colonel of a regiment
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, a great many
post is mail, letters

explanation.surface: The colonel receives a pile of mail.
explanation.walkthrough: CO (commanding officer) plus M (a thousand) plus POST (letters).
explanation.definitionFit: Rotting garden waste is piled in a mound to make fertiliser.

clue.text: Ribbed but never at odds

indicators.note: at odds means in disagreement, so the letters are out of order

explanation.surface: A remark that ribbed but never quarrelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odds' (in 'at odds') signals the anagram of NEVER AT.
explanation.definitionFit: In botany a leaf with veins is said to be veined or rib-marked.

clue.text: One roused by the cock that crowed in the morn

definitions.text: One roused by the cock that crowed in the morn

parts.words: One roused by the cock that crowed in the morn
parts.note: from the nursery rhyme This is the House that Jack Built, where the cock waked the man all shaven and shorn

explanation.definitionFit: In the rhyme the crowing bird wakes a clergyman all shaven and shorn.

clue.text: Embraced, compromised without honour

indicators.note: without tells you to take the honour out of the longer word

parts.note: OM is the Order of Merit, a British honour

explanation.surface: Someone who was hugged ends up disgraced.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' removes OM, the Order of Merit (a British honour), from COMPROMISED.
explanation.definitionFit: Comprised means included or contained, so a set embraced its parts.

clue.text: Ceremonial, we are entitled to, say ?

indicators.note: say signals the word is heard rather than written

parts.note: what we are entitled to are our rights

explanation.surface: We claim our entitlements in a formal ceremony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' gives RIGHTS heard aloud as RITES.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceremonial as a noun is the formal procedure of an occasion, its observances.

clue.text: Literal example of that, of the printer

definitions.text: Literal example of that, of the printer

parts.words: Literal example of that, of the printer
parts.note: printers call a misprint a literal, and the clue asks for the general word for such a slip

explanation.definitionFit: A literal is printers' slang for a typing mistake, one kind of mistake.

clue.text: Resting-place for a tortured torso

indicators.note: tortured says the letters of the torso are twisted into a new order

explanation.surface: A tortured body is laid out somewhere to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tortured' is the anagram signal on TORSO.
explanation.definitionFit: A perch where birds sleep is their resting spot.

clue.text: So trim a vessel to phase out

parts.note: a ship is a vessel

indicators.note: out says the letters of phase are knocked out of order

explanation.surface: A captain decides to retire an old vessel since it is so neat.
explanation.walkthrough: SHIP (vessel) is followed by PHASE rearranged, with 'out' the anagram signal and 'to' a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Neat and tidy in good order, as a well-kept sailing ship must be.

clue.text: Agent with little eye for the game

definitions.meaning: the children's game I ... begins 'I ... with my little eye'

explanation.definitionFit: A secret agent; also the guessing game I spy.

clue.text: Content, to be adequate- actor missing

indicators.note: missing tells you the player is gone from the longer word

parts.note: satisfactory means adequate
taken as written

explanation.surface: A performer is content to be merely adequate, then leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing' drops ACTOR from SATISFACTORY (adequate).
explanation.definitionFit: To content someone is to please them, meeting their wishes.

clue.text: Librettist could be a nutty character

definitions.meaning: W S ... wrote the words for the Savoy operas set by Sullivan
... the Filbert, a 1914 music-hall song figure, is 'the Knut with a K', a dandy named for a nut

explanation.walkthrough: A filbert is a hazelnut, and a 'knut' was Edwardian slang for a dandy.
explanation.definitionFit: Writer of the words for Sullivan's comic operas; also the dandy hero of the music-hall song about a hazelnut-named swell.
